question.knowledge_point: Finding the Area of an Unbounded Region
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14056069/assets/d1318686a66856057fb04027ac52ff20266e628a498458b283ee93df1e4294eb.png)

Find the total area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y={e}^{-|x|}$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{e}^{-|x|}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{e}^{-|x|}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{-|x|}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-|x|}\,\text{d}x
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{-|x|}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{x}{|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{0}-{e}^{a}) \\  & =1+0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand ${e}^{-|x|}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-|x|}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{e}^{-|x|}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{-|x|}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-|x|}\,\text{d}x \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

For q-8873, cosine cannot vanish at a solution; tan(x)=-1/2 gives roots -arctan(1/2) and \pi-arctan(1/2), whose product rounds to -1.24.
